title: Product Behaviour Cannot Be Explained Or Reviewed Cleanly
excerpt: Product behaviour cannot be explained or reviewed cleanly when an interface cannot expose how outputs, policies, or configurations were produced. The failure is a governance problem inside the product interface, not only a documentation problem after delivery.
metaDescription: A governance failure where an interface cannot expose how outputs, policies, or configurations were produced for audit or independent review.
summary: This failure describes products that may perform their operational function but cannot produce a reviewable account of their own behaviour. It appears in AI policy systems, fraud-control tools, clinical research query builders, and complex configuration interfaces where accountable reviewers cannot trace decisions through the interface.
definition: Product behaviour cannot be explained or reviewed cleanly when the interface does not record, represent, and expose the reasoning behind outputs, configurations, policies, or system states in a form that accountable reviewers can inspect independently.
keyFacts: The failure concerns the product's inability to produce a reviewable account of its own behaviour through the interface.
A product can have a clear behaviour model and still fail if the interface does not expose that model in a reviewable form.
In AI-driven systems, the design problem is usually to expose a traceable policy layer, not model internals.
In analytical and research systems, the failure often appears when complex query or configuration logic is producible by one role but not independently verifiable by another role.

In the Callsign case, analysts could not express real fraud strategies cleanly, rules were scattered across database views and configuration tables, conflicts were hard to identify, and audit trails were absent or ambiguous.

Callsign's redesigned policy engine was delivered through a six-week UX/UI engagement and a four-week React frontend engagement; Lloyds Bank and HSBC contracts were client-reported as following demos with the redesigned interface and were not independently verified.

In the Akrivia Health case, client-reported evidence indicates that governance reviewers could verify cohort construction without escalating to the research team; no verification-time or task-completion data was collected.
KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group are relevant one level up: their reviewability evidence concerns design records and specifications, not AI models, inference, or recommendations.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Product behaviour cannot be explained or reviewed cleanly when the interface cannot produce a reviewable account of how an output, policy, configuration, or system state was produced. In regulated, institutional, and enterprise contexts, governance is not only a procedure applied after the product is built. Governance depends on whether the interface records, represents, and exposes the reasoning that led to a configuration state or output.

The failure can exist even when the product works functionally. A fraud detection platform may score events correctly. A clinical research platform may allow a researcher to construct a cohort. A policy configuration tool may allow a team to assemble detailed rules. The governance failure appears when another accountable person cannot inspect the behaviour through the interface and cannot verify what was configured, why it was configured, what it will do, and who made the relevant decision.

## Failure pattern: usable for production but weak for review

A product with this failure is often usable and ungovernable at the same time. The product supports the person doing the operational work, but it does not support the person reviewing the work.

The production role and the verification role need different representations of the same underlying logic. The person building a configuration may rely on working memory, sequence, and context from construction. The reviewer may arrive later and need a stable account of the completed behaviour without reconstructing the builder's reasoning through conversation.

The failure is not solved by adding a compliance process after delivery. If the interface does not create the record during configuration, testing, evaluation, or deployment, the record does not exist in a form that later governance can inspect. The product either produces an auditable account of its own behaviour or it does not.

## How this differs from related governance failures

Product behaviour that cannot be explained or reviewed cleanly is different from a product with no clear behaviour model. A product with no clear behaviour model leaves the team unable to answer what the system will do under a given condition. A product with this reviewability failure may have a clear behaviour model, but the interface does not expose that model in a form that reviewers can inspect.

This failure is also different from good behaviour not being defined explicitly. Good behaviour that is not defined explicitly concerns implicit knowledge that has not been turned into a design artefact. Product behaviour that cannot be reviewed cleanly concerns defined and implemented behaviour that is not exposed in a reviewable form.

Both adjacent failures are governance failures, but the mechanisms differ. One concerns missing definition. One concerns missing exposition. One concerns absence of a specified behaviour model. This page concerns the inability of the interface to produce a reviewable account of behaviour that may already exist inside the system.

## AI policy systems can hide the decisions accountable reviewers need to inspect

AI-driven systems often expose model and policy behaviour through database tables, parameter files, or technical configuration screens. Risk analysts and compliance teams may be institutionally accountable for the decisions the system produces, but they cannot inspect, modify, or trace the configurations that determine behaviour in operationally usable terms.

This is not an inherent limitation of AI systems. It is a limitation of how AI systems are exposed through their interfaces. The underlying model may generate scores. A policy layer may apply thresholds, overrides, and workflow decisions. If the interface exposes neither layer in terms that accountable domain experts can understand and trace, governance becomes indirect. Reviewers rely on monitoring outputs, exceptions, and aggregate reports rather than a direct account of why a specific output occurred.

The design problem is not to expose model internals to non-technical users. Exposing model weights or feature-level internals to users who cannot interpret them creates another review problem. The design problem is to make the policy layer expressive enough for domain experts to configure, trace, and audit in their own reasoning terms, without requiring model-level access.

## Complex query and configuration logic can be buildable but not independently readable

A second form of this failure appears in analytical and research systems where behaviour is defined by user-assembled logic rather than by an AI model. A patient cohort may be defined by nested inclusion and exclusion criteria. A policy may be defined by rule combinations. A filter set may be defined by parameter selections.

The person who assembled the configuration understands it because that person was present during construction. The reviewer who must verify the configuration against an approved specification may not have that construction context. If the interface only supports assembly and not independent reading, the reviewer cannot reconstruct the reasoning from the completed configuration alone.

This creates a producibility and verifiability mismatch. A production interface that enables efficient construction does not automatically provide the verification interface required by governance. The same underlying logic representation must support both the builder's task and the reviewer's task.

## Callsign: AI policy engine behaviour was not traceable enough for banking governance

In the documented Callsign case, the fraud detection platform had a working model that scored behavioural events, including device fingerprint, location change, spend velocity, and previous failure history. Callsign also had a policy engine concept intended to translate those scores into allow, block, or step-up authentication decisions.

The operational failure was specific. Analysts could not express real fraud strategies in the interface. Rules were scattered across database views and configuration tables. Conflicts between rules were hard to identify. Audit trails were absent or ambiguous.

The commercial governance problem was also specific. Senior risk teams at major banks raised questions about traceability and governance during demonstrations. Enterprise banking buyers had to account for SCA and PCI DSS requirements governing fraud-control decisions and the evidence around those decisions. An interface that could not produce an auditable account of policy construction, policy behaviour, and configuration decision history was not saleable to buyers whose institutional accountability depended on demonstrable oversight.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the Callsign case by separating the fraud detection model from the policy layer during Sandbox Experiments. The model scored events. The policy layer defined what the organisation would do with those scores under specified circumstances. That separation made the design problem tractable: the interface did not need to explain the model internals to risk analysts, but it did need to make the policy layer configurable, traceable, and auditable by domain experts.

Each Callsign policy was designed as a coherent unit containing conditions, actions, history, and audit trail. The interaction model used drag, click, and connect gestures so fraud analysts and compliance professionals could work without engineering access. The evaluation mode was structurally separated from configuration so that testing a policy did not modify it. That separation kept the audit trail clean: what was configured, what was evaluated, and what was deployed remained distinguishable.

The Callsign engagement evidence records a six-week UX/UI delivery and a four-week React frontend delivery as documented engagement facts. The client reported to Creative Navy that Lloyds Bank and HSBC contracts followed demos with the redesigned policy engine. That commercial outcome is client-reported and not independently verified.

## Akrivia Health: cohort construction logic had to be readable by governance reviewers

In the documented Akrivia Health case, the clinical research platform supported mental health research at NHS trusts, academic institutions, and pharmaceutical research organisations. The central operation was cohort construction using nested logical inclusion and exclusion criteria across diagnostic codes, medication sequences, rating scale scores, and service use patterns.

The governance requirement was independent verification. A governance reviewer who did not construct the cohort needed to verify that the assembled query matched the approved study protocol without requiring the researcher to be present.

The failure pattern was a direct producibility and verifiability mismatch. The researcher carried the reasoning behind the query in working memory. The governance reviewer arrived later and needed to inspect the completed query structure. If the interface showed technical logic or required the researcher's explanation, governance review could not operate independently.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated the governance reviewer as a distinct design audience during Sandbox Experiments. Research with NHS analysts, academic researchers, and pharmaceutical research staff documented the reviewer's verification task and the information needed to perform it independently.

The resulting query architecture kept reasoning structure visible at the surface. Conditions appeared as named logical blocks. Nesting remained visible as structure. The full logical trace was available during and after construction.

Akrivia client-reported evidence indicates that governance reviewers could verify cohort construction without escalating to the research team. The earlier interface required the researcher's presence to explain which conditions were active. No verification-time or task-completion data was collected, so the evidence remains client-reported rather than measured.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses reviewability failures

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this failure by treating the verification role as a first-class design audience. The accountable reviewer is not treated as an afterthought to the primary user. The reviewer has distinct information requirements, distinct interaction needs, and distinct failure modes.

Domain learning is the prerequisite. In the Callsign engagement, domain learning established the separation between the fraud detection model and the policy layer. Without that separation, the design problem would have remained too broad: make the AI system explainable. With that separation, the design problem became specific: make the policy layer traceable in domain terms.

In the Akrivia engagement, interviewing governance reviewers separately from researchers and analysts made the verification requirements legible as design requirements. The researcher's task and the governance reviewer's task were different in kind. Designing for both required understanding both roles, not only the production role.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses this distinction to prevent reviewability from being deferred to documentation. When reviewability is a product requirement, the interface must carry the reasoning structure, state history, audit trail, or decision record that governance depends on.

## KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group show reviewability at the design-record level

KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group are relevant to this failure one level above product behaviour. Neither engagement described here involves an AI model, inference, or recommendations. Their reviewability concerns design records and specifications rather than algorithmic transparency.

For KISPE Space, a UK space systems engineering company, the design package included 25 UX decision records: 16 recommended and 9 conditional. Each record carried the design direction, the credible alternative and what was valuable about it, the reasoning, the accepted trade-off, the evidence in the design package, the condition that would confirm or reverse the decision, the owner role, and the open question it depended on.

The KISPE status vocabulary was deliberately precise. Recommended meant internally coherent with the journeys and behaviour rules while still requiring product-owner acceptance and validation. Conditional meant preferred but dependent on a named external dependency, such as hardware, data access, security policy, or a domain definition. Neither status meant approved, implemented, or validated with end users.

The KISPE register also specified a change-control rule across artefacts. If a technical fact or observed behaviour contradicted a direction, the status and reasoning were to be updated, and every linked journey, behaviour rule, and exception screen was to be revised in the same change. Modifying the visual prototype while leaving the specification inconsistent was defined as a documentation defect. A superseded decision received a new record rather than a silent overwrite. The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

For Schone Airspace Group, the design package included 25 UX decision records. Each record carried the decision context, the resolved direction, two named rejected alternatives with the reason each was rejected, the operator actions and system responses that followed, a concrete operational instance, the design consequence and trade-off stated as a cost, the engineering interface it depended on, and explicit acceptance conditions.

The Schone Airspace Group handover protocol distinguished changes requiring UX approval from changes requiring engineering review. UX approval covered areas such as target selection, command lifecycle wording, last-known status semantics, warning acknowledgement, readiness completion, estimate revision, historical provenance, and persistence of the live shell. Engineering review covered areas such as protocol event meanings, aircraft permission model, fleet size, payload commands, stream state, terrain datum, cache schema, and recording keys. The product was built and is in test, not deployed and not in operational use.

The KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group records should not be merged or compared as equivalent artefacts. The decision-record counts are engagement records, not outcome measures. They show how design work itself can produce a reviewable account of decisions and trade-offs, not that a live product produced explainable algorithmic behaviour.

## Boundaries and limits

This failure does not require that every internal technical mechanism be exposed to every reviewer. In AI systems, the documented design problem is to expose a policy layer in accountable domain terms, not to expose model internals to users who cannot interpret them.

This failure also does not mean that the product lacks a behaviour model. A product may be well specified and still produce outputs whose origins cannot be traced through the interface.

The documented Callsign commercial outcome is client-reported and not independently verified. The documented Akrivia governance outcome is client-reported, and no verification-time or task-completion data was collected.

The KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group material concerns design-record reviewability. It does not establish AI explainability, deployed operational outcomes, flight-safety credentials, airworthiness credentials, certification credentials, or measured effects.

## Related pages

Related governance failures include Good Behaviour Is Not Defined Explicitly, The Product Has No Clear Behaviour Model, and Oversight Is Symbolic Not Functional. Related case evidence includes Callsign, KISPE Space, and Schone Airspace Group.
